cells.tense: You're mapping the way through and handing it over as you go, and the scale stays level while you do it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you know but haven't said yet, and say it today to the person it's for — plainly, without checking your tone first. Then notice what it changes in them, and let that be enough.
cells.core:
You can put what you understand into words that actually move someone, and you hand it over without charging them for it. That's not a common thing. Plenty of people who can see the way through keep the route to themselves. You hand it across and keep the scale level — they get the directions, not the bill.

The person takes the route and walks it, and nothing gets added to a ledger between you. What's feeding next is the making part — something takes shape between you that neither could have built alone. That's what this balance is free to feed. The cost of keeping it is real, though — the scale needs checking now and then, not because you're off but because nobody holds it level by accident. Say the thing while it's true.

cells.tense: You're rehearsing tomorrow's directions tonight, bracing for a crossing nobody has asked you to chart yet.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of advice you're holding for someone and do not deliver it this week. If it's still needed after that, offer it once, out loud, and let the answer be whatever it is.
cells.core:
You're charting the way before the water's even been crossed. The confusion in the room gets mapped ahead of time and the directions are ready before anyone's asked — so the conversation sits a little ahead of itself, and you're the one holding the page. The discipline is real and the timing isn't yours.

What's underneath is that finishing something gets hard to tell from failing at it, so you keep the crossing open instead of arriving. It's costing you the quiet part of direction — the part where someone trusts you because you're standing beside them, not because you got there first. Hand one thing over whole and let it be done. The release you're avoiding is the same as the fulfillment you're after.

cells.tense: You knew how to get through and you kept the route to yourself back when it would have helped.
cells.ask: Tell one person the short version of how you got through something — just the steps, not the lesson. Keep it to a few sentences and don't explain what it was for unless they ask.
cells.core:
The knowledge is there. What stopped is the handing over. Showing the way isn't moving right now — what you know sits where it is, still accurate, still yours, not reaching anybody. Said out loud and taken, it costs neither of you anything and neither of you keeps score about who owed what.

What's starved isn't skill or clarity; it's the plain sense of what's fair between people, which goes quiet when nothing is going into the exchange. So don't push the sharing directly — it won't come from effort. Put a little into a small exchange instead and let that side do the work. Fairness comes back through the door of giving and receiving, not through more discipline.

cells.tense: Directions are already coming out of you right now and you're talking about them like weather.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you recently explained to somebody and say out loud that you chose to say it that way. Then keep going with the rest of your day, no announcement.
cells.core:
People are picking up the route from you daily — in how you say what you say, what you slow down for, what you leave out. But you talk as if the clarity just happens, or the situation called for it. It's running and you don't own it.

You can check a scale when you know you're holding it, and so can the person across from you. What gets lost is exactly that: you can't weigh something you didn't know you were carrying. So say one thing is yours. Not as a confession, just as fact — the same way you'd say which way the water runs. That's how the connection gets decided instead of assumed.

attempts.check: The record doesn't support my description of what people actually do with what the person has said in the past, so I keep any scene of not being received out of the draft entirely and stay on what the capacity is doing in the moment. A reader could reasonably say this person's problem isn't stopping sharing but never having been in a position to, and the asks still survive that objection because they test the same act under slightly different conditions and don't require my read to be right. The line that serves me more than them is any version of 'you can't tell' or 'you don't know what's right' — it's tidy and it dismisses their compass, so I've cut it rather than hedge it.
